name: Care Not Custody
headline: A broken window. Not a crime scene.
intro: Training that helps home staff and police put the DfE's 2018 national protocol into everyday decisions.

problem.scene: A slammed door ends in a 999 call.
problem.question: Then a night in custody, and a record for life.
without: A record that follows the child
with: "Good enough for my child?" asked first
Minor incidents dealt with at home
Restorative, with the child held to account
problem.standards: The DfE's national protocol (2018) asks one question of every response: would this be good enough for my child?
problem.evidence: It does not mean never calling the police. Staff still call straight away when there is a risk of serious harm.

groups: Registered managers, deputies and residential staff
Officers, neighbourhood teams, custody staff and force leads
Staff working with 16 and 17 year olds, and leaving care teams
notes: Best with home staff and police together

outcomes: Describe how an incident in a home becomes a criminal record, from the child's side and the staff member's.
Recognise signs that a child may be criminally exploited, and why that changes the response.
Explain the three levels of incident and the police options short of arrest and charge.
Use Becker's labelling theory to explain how a record changes how a child is treated and sees themselves.
Use de-escalation, a delayed response and a restorative conversation instead of calling the police by default.
Write a factual incident record with the child's account, and agree named actions with partners.

pillars.title: The national protocol's three levels of incident
pillars.stance: Would this be good enough for my child?
pillars.stance_line: The DfE's national protocol on reducing the criminalisation of children in care (2018).
items: Managed in the home, the way any family would.
Reported to the manager and the child's social worker, who decide whether police are needed.
An immediate police response, because of a risk of serious harm or significant damage.
pillars.base: Where a child may be a victim of trafficking or modern slavery, section 45 of the Modern Slavery Act 2015 can protect them from prosecution.

story_line: Four stories run through the day: Nathan, 15, Chloe, 14, Jordan, 16, and Maya, 17. Each is a composite, drawn from real experiences of care.

facilitator.name: Luke Rodgers BEM
facilitator.line: From care leaver to care leader
paras: Luke went into care at 10. He has spent his career inside children's services as a consultant, trainer and keynote speaker, and is CEO of The Care Leaders.

He has worked with councils nationally on how children's homes respond when things go wrong, including Durham, where he put NVR into 11 children's homes and helped build a strategy for the homes with 105 residential staff.
He led the national engagement on England's new fostering standards for the Department for Education, so he knows what the standards expect of the adults around a child.
He was a Knowledge Equity Fellow at Saïd Business School, University of Oxford, and was awarded the British Empire Medal in 2018 for commitment to children and families.
